passage:
Note by Mahima Sethi, music teacher, Tuesday.
Passing Class 4A at eleven o'clock, I heard the maths teacher shouting at Harish in front of everyone: 'Look at this rubbish. Even a baby could do better.' Harish stood at the board, shoulders shaking, staring at the floor. The class was dead silent. In music period he didn't sing; he sat hunched at the back. After the others left, I asked if he was okay. He whispered, 'I wanted to disappear.' I told him that being shamed like that was not his fault, and that no teacher should speak to a child that way. With his permission, I told our coordinator before lunch and phoned his father after school. His father is coming in tomorrow.

qa.q: What did the maths teacher call Harish's work?
qa.a: Rubbish.

qa.q: How did Harish feel standing at the board?
qa.a: Humiliated and ashamed; his shoulders shook, and later he said he wanted to disappear.

qa.q: What did the music teacher do that same day?
qa.a: Told Harish it wasn't his fault, reported it to the coordinator before lunch and phoned his father after school.

qa.q: How might Harish's classmates have felt during the shouting?
qa.a: Shocked and uncomfortable; the class went dead silent.

grounding: A music teacher's note records a boy humiliated by another teacher in class, and the same-day steps taken to support him.

passage:
Friday night
Dear diary, it's Tanuja. Today Maria Miss held up my crumpled homework and said to the whole class, 'This is what lazy looks like.' Everyone turned round. My face was on fire and I wanted to crawl under my desk. The homework was crumpled because the rain got into my bag on the bus, but I couldn't say it; my throat was stuck. I didn't eat my tiffin. When Mummy picked me up, I burst into tears in the auto. She held my hand the whole way home and said, 'That was not your fault. Nobody should be shamed in front of a class.' After dinner she wrote to the class teacher and the principal. I read it. It was calm. I feel a bit lighter now.

qa.q: Why was Tanuja's homework crumpled?
qa.a: The rain got into Tanuja's bag on the bus.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel when Maria Miss held up the homework?
qa.a: Humiliated and ashamed; Tanuja's face was on fire and crawling under the desk seemed better.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that same evening?
qa.a: Held Tanuja's hand, said it wasn't Tanuja's fault, and calmly wrote to the class teacher and the principal.

qa.q: What would change if Maria Miss had asked Tanuja privately about the homework?
qa.a: She could have heard about the rain, and Tanuja could have explained without being shamed.

grounding: A child shamed in front of the class writes about it, tells a parent that day, and the parent raises it with the school.

passage: In Madrid, Santiago got a lunchtime detention for 'starting a fight' in the playground. He hadn't started it. Pablo had shoved him first, and he'd only pushed back to get free. The teacher on duty had only seen the push. All afternoon, Santiago's jaw ached from clenching. On the walk home he decided not to tell Mum; she'd just be disappointed. But at dinner she asked, 'Something wrong, mi amor?' and he couldn't hold it in. He told her everything, even about his own push. Layla listened without interrupting. Then she said, 'Thank you for telling me all of it, even your part. I believe you. I'll email your teacher and ask for a proper conversation.' Santiago let out a long breath. Not every grown-up got it wrong.

qa.q: What was Santiago's detention for?
qa.a: 'Starting a fight' in the playground.

qa.q: Why did Santiago almost not tell Mum?
qa.a: He was afraid she would be disappointed in him, even though the punishment was unfair.

qa.q: Why did telling the whole story help?
qa.a: Including his own push made him believable, so Layla could see the truth and ask the teacher for a proper conversation.

qa.q: How did Layla respond to Santiago's story?
qa.a: With trust and support; she thanked him for telling all of it and said she believed him.

grounding: A boy punished unfairly at school still tells his mother the whole story, and her trust shows him not every adult misjudges.

passage: At the cricket academy, Coach benched Vishal for the whole practice match. 'Late again. No excuses.' But the city bus had broken down on the bridge, and Vishal had run the last kilometre with his kit bag bumping his back. He sat on the bench, sweat drying cold, eyes stinging. He thought about saying nothing at home. Maybe Mummy would think he'd been lazy too. When his mother, Nandini, came to pick him up, she saw his face. 'Tell me,' she said. So he did, the whole story, including that he had been late twice before for no good reason. She nodded. 'Those two times were on you. Today wasn't.' She walked over to Coach with him, and Vishal showed the bus ticket with the time on it. Coach frowned, then said, 'All right. Next match, you're in.'

qa.q: Where did the city bus break down?
qa.a: On the bridge.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling on the bench?
qa.a: Hurt and unfairly treated; his eyes stung, and he worried Mummy might think he was lazy too.

qa.q: How did trusting his mother help?
qa.a: Telling her everything, even his earlier lateness, let her back him fairly and go with him to show Coach the bus ticket.

qa.q: How did Coach respond once he saw the ticket?
qa.a: He reconsidered and put Vishal in the next match.

grounding: At a cricket academy a boy punished unfairly tells his mother the whole truth, and she helps him be heard.

passage: In Leeds, the grown-ups had decided. At parents' evening, Emeka's parents and his teacher agreed he would stop art club and do extra maths on Wednesdays instead. Nobody asked him. Art club was the best hour of his week. That night he lay in bed with his fists tight, thinking about scribbling all over the maths worksheets so they'd see. But he knew that would only make things worse. On Saturday, at Auntie Clara's flat, he finally said it out loud. 'I feel like I don't count. They just decide.' Auntie Clara listened, then asked, 'What would you want to say to them?' Together they wrote it down. On Sunday, Emeka asked his parents, politely, for ten minutes. They listened. They agreed to try maths on Mondays and keep art.

qa.q: What did the grown-ups decide at parents' evening?
qa.a: That Emeka would stop art club and do extra maths on Wednesdays.

qa.q: How did Emeka feel lying in bed with his fists tight?
qa.a: Helpless and angry, as if he didn't count, because nobody had asked him.

qa.q: What worked better than scribbling on the worksheets?
qa.a: Naming the feeling to Auntie Clara, writing down what he wanted to say, and politely asking his parents for ten minutes.

qa.q: How might Emeka's parents have felt when he asked to talk?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised, but willing; they listened and changed the plan.

grounding: A boy who feels powerless when adults decide for him names the feeling to a safe adult and asks politely to be heard.

passage: At the residential school, the list went up on Sunday: Ujjwal was moving from Dorm 3 to Dorm 7, away from every friend he had. Nobody had asked him. When he went to the warden's office, the answer was short: 'Decided. Pack by tonight.' Ujjwal stood in the corridor, throat thick. He couldn't argue. He thought about hiding his trunk, or letting the air out of the warden's cycle tyres. Instead he found Payal Didi, the house mother, folding towels. 'I feel like I don't get any say in anything here,' he said, his voice cracking. Payal Didi put the towels down. 'That's a hard feeling. Shall we ask the warden, politely, why, and whether one friend can move with you?' They went together. The warden explained that Dorm 3 needed repairs, and agreed that his friend Sanju could move too.

qa.q: Which dorm was Ujjwal moved to?
qa.a: Dorm 7.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling in the corridor?
qa.a: Helpless and upset, with a thick throat, because the decision was made without him.

qa.q: What choice did Ujjwal make instead of revenge?
qa.a: He named his feeling to Payal Didi and went with her to ask the warden politely for a reason and a small change.

qa.q: How might the warden see Ujjwal's polite request?
qa.a: As reasonable; the warden explained about the repairs and let his friend Sanju move too.

grounding: At a residential school a boy who feels powerless over a dorm move tells a safe adult and asks politely to be heard.

passage: In the village school outside Satara, the new box of chalk vanished from Guruji's table during recess. Vasudha had been sitting nearest the window, so Guruji made her stand in the corner for the rest of the morning. Her ears were red, and she kept blinking hard. Omkar's heart pounded. He had seen what happened: a monkey had jumped through the window, grabbed the box and bounded up the neem tree. But Guruji looked cross, and nobody spoke. At lunch, Omkar walked quietly to Guruji's table, hands sweating. 'Guruji, it wasn't Vasudha. I saw a monkey take it. It's up the neem tree.' Guruji went to the window, squinted, and saw bits of chalk scattered below. He called Vasudha out of the corner and apologised to her.

qa.q: Where did the monkey take the chalk box?
qa.a: Up the neem tree.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel before speaking to Guruji?
qa.a: Nervous but full of compassion; his heart pounded and his hands were sweating, yet he couldn't let Vasudha be punished unfairly.

qa.q: Why was Omkar's way of speaking up a good one?
qa.a: He went quietly to Guruji at lunch with the facts, so Guruji could check without a scene.

qa.q: What was it like for Vasudha standing in the corner?
qa.a: Humiliating and unfair; her ears were red and she kept blinking hard.

grounding: A village boy who knows a classmate was punished unfairly quietly tells the teacher the truth, despite his fear.

passage: In Abebe's class in Addis Ababa, someone had written a rude word on the blackboard before the teacher came in. The teacher saw chalk dust on Vera's sleeve and kept her in at break to clean all the boards. Abebe knew the truth. Vera had only been writing the date, like every morning. It was Dawit who had scrawled the word, laughing, while Vera was at the tap. Abebe's stomach churned. Dawit was big and had many friends. But Vera's face was pale, and she wasn't even arguing. When the bell rang, Abebe waited until the others had gone. 'Teacher, please, Vera didn't write it. She was at the tap. I saw someone else do it.' The teacher looked at him for a long moment, then went over to talk to Vera.

qa.q: What did the teacher see on Vera's sleeve?
qa.a: Chalk dust.

qa.q: Why did Abebe's stomach churn?
qa.a: He was scared of Dawit, but upset and sorry for Vera, who was being punished for something she didn't do.

qa.q: How did Abebe speak up in a brave but careful way?
qa.a: He waited until the others had gone and quietly told the teacher that Vera didn't do it, without making a scene.

qa.q: How might Vera feel when the teacher came to talk to her?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, after staying pale and silent while wrongly punished.

grounding: A boy who knows the truth quietly speaks up for a classmate punished for something she did not do.

passage: Last Thursday, Aiko Sensei had marked Fatima's science project late and taken off points, though Fatima had put it on her desk on time. The next Monday, after class, Aiko Sensei called her over. 'Fatima, I found your project under the pile of worksheets. It was on time. I was wrong, and I'm sorry. I've fixed the mark.' Fatima's shoulders dropped with relief. But a small sore feeling stayed, like a bruise when you press it. For four days she had believed she was careless. She could stay cold. She thought about it on the walk home past the canal in Kyoto. Aiko Sensei had said sorry plainly, without excuses. The next morning, Fatima bowed a little and said, 'Thank you for telling me, Sensei.' The sore feeling faded faster after that.

qa.q: Where did Aiko Sensei find the project?
qa.a: Under the pile of worksheets.

qa.q: How did Fatima feel after the apology?
qa.a: Relieved, but still a little sore, like a bruise when pressed.

qa.q: What helped the sore feeling fade?
qa.a: Accepting the plain, sincere apology and thanking the teacher, instead of staying cold.

qa.q: How might Aiko Sensei have felt apologising?
qa.a: Regretful and a bit embarrassed, but honest enough to admit the mistake and fix it.

grounding: A girl in Japan receives her teacher's sincere apology for an unfair mark, feels relieved but sore, and forgives gently.

passage: At the Bharatanatyam academy, Sunaina Ma'am had moved Ritu from the front row to the back after the dress rehearsal. 'You clearly haven't practised,' she'd said in front of everyone. Ritu had practised every evening; her ankle bells had simply come untied mid-step. For a week Ritu danced at the back, tight in the chest. Then, after Saturday's class, Sunaina Ma'am sat down beside her on the wooden floor. 'I watched the rehearsal video. Your bells came loose. I was wrong to say you hadn't practised. I'm sorry, Ritu.' Ritu felt relief rush up her throat, and a sting behind it. Part of her wanted to say, 'It's too late.' Instead she said, 'Thank you, Ma'am.' Walking home, her feet felt lighter. Sunaina Ma'am was human too.

qa.q: What came untied mid-step?
qa.a: Ritu's ankle bells.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when Sunaina Ma'am apologised?
qa.a: Relieved, with a sting of hurt still behind it; part of her wanted to say it was too late.

qa.q: Why was accepting the apology a good choice for Ritu?
qa.a: Forgiving gently let her stop carrying the anger, and her feet felt lighter walking home 😊

qa.q: What might Sunaina Ma'am have felt after watching the video?
qa.a: Regretful and sorry for judging Ritu too quickly in front of everyone.

grounding: At a dance academy a girl's teacher admits she was wrong, and the girl accepts the apology despite still feeling sore.

passage:
Note from Trisha Masi, staying with the family this week.
This evening Didi saw the broken vase and, without asking, took away Indu's cycle for a week. Indu shouted, 'It's not fair! You never listen!' and ran to her room, slamming the door. I sat with her after a while. She was crying into her pillow. 'It was the cat, Masi. I was only picking up the pieces.' I told her that shouting when you feel wronged is natural, but that her parents might hear her better once everyone was calm. After twenty minutes she washed her face and went to the kitchen. 'Mummy, can I say my side, calmly?' Didi put the ladle down and listened. The cycle was back before dinner.

qa.q: What punishment did Didi give Indu?
qa.a: She took away Indu's cycle for a week.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when she shouted and slammed the door?
qa.a: Angry and wronged, because she was punished before anyone heard her side.

qa.q: What helped Indu get heard?
qa.a: Cooling down for a while, then asking to share her side calmly with her mother.

qa.q: How might Indu's mother have felt after listening?
qa.a: Sorry for rushing to punish, since she gave the cycle back before dinner.

grounding: An aunt's note describes a girl punished before being heard, who shouts, then cools down and explains calmly.

passage:
Sunday
Diary, Uday writing. Today I came home an hour late from the park, and Papa didn't even let me take my shoes off. 'No TV for a week. You never think of anyone.' I shouted, 'You don't even know what happened!' and he said, 'Don't raise your voice.' I stomped off. The truth is, Varun had wandered off near the lake, and I spent the whole hour searching with the park guard until we found him by the swings. I was scared stiff. I sat on the terrace, steaming. After a while my breathing slowed. I went downstairs and said, 'Papa, can I tell you why I was late? Calmly?' He nodded. When I finished, he rubbed his face and said, 'I'm sorry I didn't ask first.' No-TV week is cancelled.

qa.q: Who helped Uday search for Varun?
qa.a: The park guard.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling on the terrace?
qa.a: Angry and wronged, steaming at being punished before explaining, after being scared stiff searching for Varun.

qa.q: What did Uday do that got Papa to listen?
qa.a: Waited until calmer, then asked to explain once, calmly.

qa.q: How did Papa feel after hearing the reason?
qa.a: Sorry; he rubbed his face and apologised for not asking first.

grounding: A child punished before being heard shouts in protest, then cools down and explains calmly, and the parent listens.

passage: Tomas walked out of his Lisbon school with the report card in his backpack like a stone. Maths: a big red 2 out of 5. Dad had been so proud of the last one. On the tram, he imagined Dad's face falling, the long sigh. He thought about hiding the card under his mattress until the end of term. His friend Tariq, beside him, said, 'I hid mine last year. Mum found it in a month. It was ten times worse.' Tomas stared out at the river. At home, before he could lose his nerve, he laid the card on the kitchen table. 'Dad, my maths is bad. I've thought about it. Can I ask Senhora Costa for extra help on Tuesdays?' Dad read it, sighed once, and then pulled out a chair. 'Tell me what went wrong.'

qa.q: What mark did Tomas get in maths?
qa.a: A 2 out of 5.

qa.q: What was Tomas afraid of on the tram?
qa.a: He was afraid of Dad's disappointment, imagining his face falling and the long sigh.

qa.q: Why did Tomas's approach at home work well?
qa.a: He showed the card early and came with a calm plan, extra help on Tuesdays, instead of hiding it.

qa.q: How might Dad have felt when Tomas showed the card with a plan?
qa.a: Disappointed at first, but reassured by Tomas's honesty, so he sat down to talk.

grounding: A boy dreading his father's disappointment over a report card shares it early with a calm plan instead of hiding it.

passage: Results day, and the school hall buzzed with parents on plastic chairs. Mehak clutched her mark sheet: her worst science mark ever. Ammi would be here in ten minutes for the parent-teacher meeting. Mehak's hands were cold. She pictured Ammi's face when Ma'am read the mark out. 'Just don't show her,' Ayesha whispered. 'Say they haven't come yet.' But Ma'am had the list anyway. Mehak went to the gate and waited. When Ammi arrived, Mehak handed her the sheet before they walked in. 'Ammi, science went badly. I got confused in the electricity chapter. I want to redo those exercises with you on Sundays.' Ammi read it, then looked at her. 'Thank you for telling me first.' They walked in together.

qa.q: Which chapter confused Mehak?
qa.a: The electricity chapter.

qa.q: Why were Mehak's hands cold?
qa.a: She was scared of Ammi's disappointment, picturing her face when Ma'am read the mark out.

qa.q: What did Mehak do instead of hiding the result?
qa.a: Showed Ammi first at the gate and offered a plan to redo the exercises on Sundays.

qa.q: How did Ammi feel about hearing it from Mehak first?
qa.a: Grateful and trusting; she thanked Mehak and walked in with her.

grounding: On results day a girl afraid of her mother's disappointment shows her the mark sheet first, with a plan.

passage: At the school's prize day, Pema walked up to the stage for the first-in-class cup, and in the third row her parents stood up and clapped so loudly the principal laughed. Afterwards, in the crowded courtyard, Papa told every parent who passed, 'Our Pema, first again!' Her mother, Jyoti, took twelve photos of the cup. Pema's cheeks hurt from smiling. But a small cold thought crept in: what if next year I'm second? At the samosa stall she tugged Mummy's sleeve. 'What if I don't come first next time?' Mummy knelt down. 'Then I'll still be proud that you worked hard, and prouder that you're kind to Norbu.' She nodded at Pema's classmate by the stall. Pema let out a breath and bit into her samosa.

qa.q: How many photos did Jyoti take of the cup?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling behind her smiles in the courtyard?
qa.a: Happy, but also worried and pressured, afraid of coming second next year.

qa.q: What helped Pema with the pressure?
qa.a: Asking Mummy directly and hearing that she is valued for hard work and kindness, not just rank.

qa.q: How does Papa experience the day?
qa.a: As a proud, joyful moment he wants to share with everyone 🎉

grounding: At prize day a girl enjoys her parents' pride but feels pressure, and is reassured that her worth is more than her rank.

passage:
Wednesday. Tarun's results came: 96 percent. Mummy cried happy tears and Papa phoned every relative, even the ones in Canada. Tarun felt like a balloon, floating.
Saturday. At the family lunch, Papa told everyone again. Chachu said, 'Next year, 100!' Everyone laughed. Tarun smiled, but his stomach tightened. What if he got 90 next year? Would they stop phoning people?
Monday. At the cricket nets, his friend Francis said, 'You're quiet. Aren't you happy?' 'I am. I'm also scared,' Tarun admitted. That evening he told Mummy the same thing. She hugged him. 'We're proud of you, not just of a number.' Tarun decided to enjoy it, and to remember what she said.

qa.q: What did Chachu say at the family lunch?
qa.a: 'Next year, 100!'

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling after Chachu's comment?
qa.a: Pressured and scared; his stomach tightened as he wondered what would happen with a lower mark next year.

qa.q: What did Tarun do with the mixed feelings?
qa.a: He admitted them to Francis and then to Mummy, who said they are proud of him, not just of a number.

qa.q: How did Mummy feel on results day?
qa.a: Overjoyed; she cried happy tears.

grounding: Over several days a boy enjoys his parents' pride in his marks but feels pressure, and says so.

passage: 'Ojas, your mother sighed over your report and mentioned your cousin, and now you feel like nothing? Sit with your Dilnaz Aunty. When I was ten, my father read my report card at the dining table and said, "Rustom got a distinction. What happened to you?" I felt about as big as a grain of rice. I wanted to shout that Rustom had a tutor and I didn't. Instead I cried in the bathroom. Later my grandmother told me, "Your father worries loudly. That's his fear, not your worth." The next morning I said to him, "Pappa, I'll work harder at maths, but I need help, and please don't compare me." He was quiet a long while. Then he found me a tutor. And he stopped saying Rustom's name at dinner.'

qa.q: What did Rustom get?
qa.a: A distinction.

qa.q: How did young Dilnaz feel when her father compared her with Rustom?
qa.a: Small and hurt, about as big as a grain of rice.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped young Dilnaz keep her self-respect?
qa.a: Asking her father for help and asking him not to compare her, instead of shouting.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz's grandmother see behind the father's words?
qa.a: His own anxious worry, not a judgment of Dilnaz's worth.

grounding: An aunt recalls her father comparing her marks with a cousin's, and asking for help without losing her self-respect.

passage: The car had been stuck in traffic on the highway for forty minutes, and Mummy was reading Zubin's report card again. She sighed. 'Vijay got an A in every subject. You're both in the same class, same school.' Papa sighed too. Zubin looked out at the rain on the window, feeling tiny. And they were on their way to Vijay's house for Diwali, where the whole family would ask about marks. His throat ached. Then he remembered what his teacher had said: worried parents don't mean bad kids. He took a breath. 'Mummy, I know my maths is weak. I'll try harder, and can you help me find a tutor? But when you compare me with Vijay, I feel like nothing.' The car went quiet. Mummy folded the report card away. 'Fair,' she said softly.

qa.q: How long had the car been stuck in traffic?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling as he looked at the rain?
qa.a: Tiny and hurt, and dreading the relatives' questions about marks at Vijay's house.

qa.q: How did Zubin speak up without losing his self-respect?
qa.a: He admitted his weak maths, promised to try and asked for a tutor, and told his parents how the comparison made him feel.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt after Zubin spoke?
qa.a: Surprised and sorry; she folded the report card away and said 'fair' softly.

grounding: Stuck in traffic, a boy whose parents sigh and compare him with his cousin asks for help and says how it feels.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 6B, results day.
When I read out that Francis had come first, Kalyani, his closest friend, clapped more slowly than the others. At break I heard her tell two girls, 'He only topped because he sits in front and sucks up.' She looked miserable saying it. Later she stayed back and admitted, 'It felt like a punch in my stomach. I wanted to be first.' I told her the sting is normal and shows she cares about doing well, but that running Francis down would hurt them both. I suggested she ask him how he revised. At lunch I saw them together, Francis drawing a revision timetable in her notebook. Kalyani was nodding.

qa.q: Who came first in the class?
qa.a: Francis.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she said Francis only topped because he sucks up?
qa.a: Envious and miserable; it felt like a punch in the stomach because she wanted to be first.

qa.q: What did the teacher suggest, and what did Kalyani do?
qa.a: To ask Francis how he revised; at lunch he drew a revision timetable in her notebook.

qa.q: How might Francis feel if he heard Kalyani's comment?
qa.a: Hurt and confused that his closest friend had run him down.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a girl envious of her friend topping the class, and turning envy into learning from him.

passage:
Thursday
Diary, it's Samir. Jatin topped the whole class in science. Ninety-eight! When Ma'am said his name, I felt a sharp jab in my belly, like I'd swallowed a wasp. I got eighty-one. We study together every Sunday, so how? At lunch I almost told Akash that Jatin probably saw the paper early. I stopped halfway, because that was mean and not even true. Then I felt worse. After school I asked Jatin straight out, 'What did you do differently?' He said he made his own quiz cards and tested himself every night instead of just reading. He even offered to make some for me. I'm still a bit jealous. But I'm going to try the cards. On Sunday we're making them together.

qa.q: What did Jatin make to study?
qa.a: His own quiz cards.

qa.q: How did Samir feel when Ma'am said Jatin's name?
qa.a: A sharp jab of envy in the belly, like having swallowed a wasp.

qa.q: What turned Samir's envy into something useful?
qa.a: Asking Jatin what he did differently and planning to try his quiz-card method.

qa.q: How did Jatin respond to Samir's question?
qa.a: Generously; he explained his method and offered to make cards for Samir.

grounding: A child stung by envy when a friend tops the class stops short of running him down and asks what helped him study.
